glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To move upwards.

examples.text: We watched the balloon rise.
Disturbed by my footsteps, the birds rose above the treetops.

glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To grow upward; to attain a certain height.

examples.text: This elm tree rises to a height of seventy feet.

glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To slope upward.

examples.text: The path rises as you approach the foot of the hill.

glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To appear to move upwards from behind the horizon of a planet as a result of the planet's rotation.

examples.text: And still the hours passed, and at last I knew by the glimmer of light in the tomb above that the sun had risen again, and a maddening thirst had hold of me. And then I thought of all the barrels piled up in the vault and of the liquor that they held; and stuck not because 'twas spirit, for I would scarce have paused to sate that thirst even with molten lead.
The sun was rising in the East.

glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To become erect; to assume an upright position.

examples.text: to rise from a chair or from a fall

glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To leave one's bed; to get up.

examples.text:
Yellow is the colour of my true love's hair,
In the morning, when we rise

glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To be resurrected.

examples.text: he rose from the grave;   he is risen!

glosses: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To terminate an official sitting; to adjourn.

examples.text: The committee rose after agreeing to the report.
It was near nine[…]before the House rose.

glosses: To increase in value or standing.
To attain a higher status.

examples.text: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall.
among the rising theologians of Germany
Caesar Enrico “Rico” Bandello is a hoodlum who rises swiftly in Chicago’s mob world, in the 1931 film “Little Caesar.” Played by Edward G. Robinson, Rico is tracked down by police and shot.

glosses: To increase in value or standing.
Of a quantity, price, etc., to increase.

examples.text: Investors face a quandary. Cash offers a return of virtually zero in many developed countries; government-bond yields may have risen in recent weeks but they are still unattractive. Equities have suffered two big bear markets since 2000 and are wobbling again. It is hardly surprising that pension funds, insurers and endowments are searching for new sources of return.

glosses: To increase in value or standing.
To become more and more dignified or forcible; to increase in interest or power; said of style, thought, or discourse.

examples.text: to rise in force of expression; to rise in eloquence; a story rises in interest.

The humor of my proposition appealed more strongly to Miss Trevor than I had looked for, and from that time forward she became her old self again;[…]. Our table in the dining-room became again the abode of scintillating wit and caustic repartee, Farrar bracing up to his old standard, and the demand for seats in the vicinity rose to an animated competition.

glosses: To increase in value or standing.
To ascend on a musical scale; to take a higher pitch.

examples.text: to rise a tone or semitone

glosses: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
To become active, effective or operational, especially in response to an external or internal stimulus.

examples.text: to rise to the occasion
Thus far, my intellect has been able to rise sufficiently to meet every academic challenge that I have encountered.
As Patrick continued to goad me, I felt my temper rising towards the limits of my self control.

Professor Peter Crome, chair of the audit's steering group, said the report "provides further concrete evidence that the care of patients with dementia in hospital is in need of a radical shake-up". While a few hospitals had risen to the challenge of improving patients' experiences, many have not, he said. The report recommends that all staff receive basic dementia awareness training, and staffing levels should be maintained to help such patients.

glosses: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
To develop, to come about or intensify.

examples.text: As hunger and despondency became more intense, a determination rose within me to find a way of getting off the desert island.

To-night the winds begin to rise
⁠And roar from yonder dropping day:
⁠The last red leaf is whirl’d away,
The rooks are blown about the skies; […]

glosses: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
To swell or puff up in the process of fermentation; to become light.

examples.text: Has that dough risen yet?

glosses: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
To have its source (in a particular place).

examples.text: The majestic Marannon, or Amazon River, rises out of the Lake Launcocha, situated in the province of Tarma, in 10° 14ʹ south latitude, and ten leagues to the north of Pasco.

glosses: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
To become perceptible to the senses (other than sight).

examples.text: a noise rose on the air; odour rises from the flower

glosses: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
To become agitated, opposed, or hostile; to go to war; to take up arms; to rebel.

examples.text:
At our heels all hell should rise
 With blackest insurrection.
No more ſhall nation againſt nation riſe, / Nor ardent vvarriours meet vvith hateful eyes, […]

glosses: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
To come to mind; to be suggested; to occur.

examples.text: A thought rose in me, which I believe very often perplexes […]men of contemplative natures.

glosses: To go up; to ascend; to climb.

examples.text: to rise a hill

glosses: To cause to go up or ascend.

examples.text: to rise a fish, or cause it to come to the surface of the water
to rise a ship, or bring it above the horizon by approaching it
Until we rose the bark we could not pretend to call it a chase.

glosses: To retire; to give up a siege.

examples.text: He,[…] rising with small honour from Gunza,[…]was gone.

glosses: To come; to offer itself.

examples.text: There chaunced to the Princes hand to rize, / An auncient booke, […]

glosses: To be lifted, or capable of being lifted, from the imposing stone without dropping any of the type; said of a form.

examples.text: One side of the form is now to be lifted from the stone just enough to allow the compositor to see whether it will rise or not but not so high as to let any loose letters drop out.

glosses: The process of or an action or instance of moving upwards or becoming greater.

examples.text: The rise of the tide.
There was a rise of nearly two degrees since yesterday.
Exercise is usually accompanied by a temporary rise in blood pressure.

glosses: The process of or an action or instance of coming to prominence.

examples.text: The rise of the working class.
The rise of the printing press.
The rise of the feminists.

glosses: An increase in a quantity, price, etc.
Ellipsis of pay rise (“an increase in wage or salary”).

examples.text: The governor just gave me a rise of two pound six.

glosses: The amount of material extending from waist to crotch in a pair of trousers or shorts.

examples.text: The rise of his pants was so low that his tailbone was exposed.

glosses: The front of a diaper.
A small hill; used chiefly in place names.
An area of terrain that tends upward away from the viewer, such that it conceals the region behind it; a slope.

examples.text: the land rolls gently, so that, upon cresting a low rise or passing a copse of wind turbines, you suddenly spot a lot full of lorries or a complex of gigantic sheds.
I went along up the bank with one eye out for pap and t'other one out for what the rise might fetch along.

glosses: A very noticeable visible or audible reaction of a person or group.

examples.text: Making fun of their football team is one sure way to get a rise from a crowd.
She really got a rise from the audience when she donned a wig and talked like the president.

glosses: The height of an arch or a step.

examples.text: As the rise, i.e. height, of the arch decreases, the outward thrust increases.
Each step had a rise of 170 mm and a going of 250 mm.

glosses: Alternative form of rice (“twig”).

glosses: To rebel, particularly against authority.

examples.text: Our diſcontented Counties doe reuolt
The farmers had to revolt against the government to get what they deserved.

glosses: To repel greatly.

examples.text: Your brother revolts me!
I shall be told, that this abominable medley is made rather to revolt young and ingenuous minds.

1870, John Morley, Condorcet (published in the Fortnightly Review
To derive delight from what inflicts pain on any sentient creature revolted his conscience and offended his reason.

glosses: To be disgusted, shocked, or grossly offended; hence, to feel nausea; used with at.

examples.text: The stomach revolts at such food; his nature revolts at cruelty.

glosses: To cause to turn back; to roll or drive back; to put to flight.

examples.text: The foring clouds into fad fhowres y molt; / So to her yold the flames, and did their force reuolt.

glosses: To turn away; to abandon or reject something; specifically, to turn away, or shrink, with abhorrence.

examples.text: And ſtill revolt when truth would ſet them free.
His clear intelligence revolted from the dominant sophisms of that time.

glosses: An act of revolting.

examples.text:
— It's a revolt?
— No, Sire, it's a revolution...
